title: A Speedometer for Change
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece treats the pace of organizational change as a deliberate leadership variable rather than a fixed setting, weighing the tradeoffs between slow, transition-style change and fast, momentum-driven change. Slow change tends to stick better and build buy-in but risks losing energy and letting resistance organize; fast change builds momentum and energy but produces more discomfort and leaves behind team members who can't keep pace. The essay's practical takeaway is that most real organizational change blends both speeds -- quick on rationale and strategy, slower on execution -- and that leaders should continuously recalibrate pace against a single guiding question about resistance and acceptance.
points: The pace of organizational change is a deliberate leadership choice, not a fixed constant -- and it directly shapes resistance and acceptance.
Slow change (transition) tends to have more lasting power but risks losing momentum and giving antagonists room to organize.
Fast change builds energizing momentum but produces more resistance and can leave some team members behind.
Most real organizational change blends both speeds: quick on strategy and rationale, slower on execution.
The guiding question for pacing change is how to reduce resistance and increase acceptance -- and the right answer shifts over time.
quotes: Introducing and executing a change within an organization is as much art as it is science.
Because the pace of change influences resistance and acceptance, establishing the best cadence for a given change is of the utmost importance for leaders.
Slow change is more likely to stick because it affords leaders the time they need to get people involved and to participate actively in the change.
As a rule, however, the faster the change, the more resistance it produces.
The best leaders break for curves and hit the accelerator when the road is straight and clear.
